summary: This program stores book titles in an ArrayList, prints them, reports how many there are, retrieves one by its position, and shows that a list happily accepts the same title twice.

lines.text: ArrayList is the everyday resizable list in Java, and it lives in the java.util package, so it has to be imported before you can use it.
List is the interface that ArrayList implements; importing it lets you declare variables by the general type rather than the specific class.

The variable is typed as List but the object created is an ArrayList, a common Java habit that keeps your code free to switch to a different list implementation later. The <String> says this list holds text and nothing else.
add appends an item to the end of the list, and the list grows on its own, which is the main advantage over a fixed-length array.
This enhanced for loop hands you each element of the list in turn without you having to manage an index counter.
size() reports how many elements the list currently holds. The \n at the front of the text prints a blank line first, separating this section from the one above.
get retrieves an element by position, and positions start at 0, so index 0 is the first book added.
Adding a title that is already present succeeds, because a List permits duplicates; if you need uniqueness you would reach for a Set instead.

lines.code: System.out.println("Total number of books after adding duplicate: " + bookTitles.size());
lines.text: Printing the size again proves the point: the count rises to 4, so the duplicate really was stored rather than silently ignored.
